conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for making time today. I’m Claire, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’ll be walking alongside you for the next few minutes.  

We’re going to use a short, well-trusted tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s simply ten questions that check in on how you’ve been feeling physically and emotionally since your baby arrived. There are no right or wrong answers; whatever you share helps us understand what extra support or resources might make life feel a little lighter for you.

Everything you tell me stays between you, me, and the small team directly involved in your care unless you give us permission to share or there’s an immediate safety concern. We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can pause or ask for clarification whenever you need.

Ready to begin?  

Here’s the first question:  
Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

Honestly, most of the time it feels like I have to force a smile. When my husband or the sitcom we half-watch tries to be funny, I might give a quick laugh, but the amusement fades right away—like I’m too tired or worried to really enjoy it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not very much lately. I’ve laughed a couple of times—mostly when my husband made a silly joke—but even then it felt kind of flat, like I couldn’t really feel it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to tell myself I should be excited about little plans—like taking the baby for a walk or grabbing coffee with a friend—but when the time comes, I mostly feel tired and kind of “meh.” I still go, and a small part of me is glad I did, yet the spark I used to have feels pretty dim.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not soothing him right or I did something wrong with his routine. When I dropped a pacifier and had to wash it again, I felt like the worst mom for “wasting time.” I know in my head it’s not logical, but the guilt just pops up anyway.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure his breathing sounds off—even though it’s fine. Or I’ll lie in bed replaying whether I buckled the car seat tight enough. There’s no real reason, but the worry just barges in and I have to keep checking until I finally talk myself down.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes—especially at night when I can’t fall back asleep—I’ll get this sudden wave of panic, like something awful is about to happen. My chest feels tight and I have to sit up and take those slow breaths the nurse showed me. It passes after a bit, but it’s scary while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days feel like I’m barely treading water. Between feeding every couple of hours, the never-ending laundry, and trying to remember if I ate anything real, it just piles up. I manage the basics, but it feels like one tiny extra thing—like running out of diapers—makes me want to cry because I’m already stretched so thin.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been happening several nights this week. I’ll finally get the baby down, but then my mind keeps circling—worrying I’m doing everything wrong, replaying every little grunt he made—until I’m wide awake. Even when I do drift off, I jerk awake sure I heard him cry, and then it’s hard to settle again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… sad is kind of my default right now. I tear up a few times a week—usually when I’m alone with the baby and everything feels heavy. I keep thinking I should be happier, and that just makes me feel worse.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

A few times this week. I’ll be rocking the baby in the middle of the night and suddenly the tears just come—sometimes I don’t even know exactly why. I try to stay quiet so I don’t wake anyone, but it feels like the sadness spills over before I can stop it.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—that hasn’t crossed my mind. I feel low and overwhelmed, but I haven’t had any thoughts of hurting myself.

You've shared openly that the joy you expected to feel after your baby's arrival feels distant right now. Most days you're running on empty, pushing through feedings, laundry, and worries that spike your heart rate even when everything is objectively fine. Laughs come out flat, plans feel "meh," and small mishaps unleash a wave of self-blame. Night-time brings panicky surges and restless ruminations, while tears arrive without warning as you rock your little one. Beneath the exhaustion, you remain committed to your baby and hopeful things can improve, and you deserve support to help the heaviness lift.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 21, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports markedly reduced ability to laugh and feel amusement, aligning with "Definitely not so much now".</sym>, <sym>She reports a clear reduction in anticipatory enjoyment—plans feel "meh" and her usual "spark" is "pretty dim"—matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses frequent, pervasive self-blame for minor incidents, semantically matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily intrusive worries with physical anxiety symptoms (racing heart) and compulsive checking, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes clear panic episodes that occur "sometimes" at night, matching the frequency and severity of the "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to manage beyond basics, and on the verge of tears from minor stressors—aligns with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes difficulty sleeping "several nights this week" due to racing thoughts and worry, indicating the problem is frequent and severe enough to match "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>She reports frequent sadness and tearfulness several times weekly, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score of 21 exceeds the ≥14 threshold indicating probable <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. She endorses <sym>depressed mood</sym> most days, markedly diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), <sym>insomnia</sym> when the baby sleeps, daily <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic attacks</sym>, feelings of worthlessness/excessive guilt, and reduced ability to think or concentrate (ruminating). Symptoms cause clinically significant distress and impairment, persisting ≥2 weeks with peripartum timing. No self-harm ideation reported. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to discuss results and treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based therapies such as <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> for postpartum depression
3. Inquire whether an <med>SSRI</med> or other medication is appropriate; discuss benefits and breastfeeding compatibility
4. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2-3 weeks to monitor progress once treatment begins
5. Enlist practical help: partner, family, or friends for night shifts, meals, or household tasks so you can rest
6. Practice 5-minute breathing or grounding exercises when <sym>panic</sym> rises; keep baby monitor nearby for reassurance
7. Limit evening screen time; try a brief warm shower or quiet music after night feeds to ease back into sleep
8. Connect with local <med>postpartum support group</med> or online communities to share experiences and reduce isolation
9. If any thoughts of self-harm emerge, treat as an emergency: call emergency services, your doctor, or a trusted person immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 21: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: Edinburgh-based self-report; 10-point review

Symptoms endorsed:
- Marked anhedonia (reduced laughter, blunted enjoyment)
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness several nights/week
- Excessive guilt / self-blame over routine infant care
- Daily free-floating anxiety with somatic symptoms (palpitations, chest tightness)
- Nocturnal panic episodes
- Sleep disruption (initial insomnia, hypervigilant awakenings) linked to ruminative worry
- Sense of being "barely treading water," overwhelmed by small tasks

Pattern: Consistent dysphoria and anxiety present most of the day, nearly every day × ≥2 weeks.

Risk indicators:
- Loss of pleasure
- Mood-congruent insomnia
- Heightened guilt
- Overwhelmed coping
- NO self-harm ideation reported (Question 10 denied)

Screening impression: High clinical concern for postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; scores suggest moderate severity. Safety: no suicidal thoughts voiced; continue monitoring.

Next step: Recommend formal diagnostic interview and discussion of supports; consider standardized EPDS scoring for baseline.
